{{Short description|Number that has more digits than the number of digits in its prime factorization}}
In [[number theory]], a '''frugal number''' is a [[natural number]] in a given [[number base]] that has more [[numerical digit|digits]] than the number of digits in its [[prime factorization]] in the given number base (including exponents).<ref name="Darling102">{{cite book |title=The universal book of mathematics: from Abracadabra to Zeno's paradoxes |last=Darling |first=David J. |year=2004 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=978-0-471-27047-8 |page=102 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nnpChqstvg0C&pg=PA102 }}</ref> For example, in [[base 10]], 125 = 5<sup>3</sup>, 128 = 2<sup>7</sup>, 243 = 3<sup>5</sup>, and 256 = 2<sup>8</sup> are frugal numbers {{OEIS|id=A046759}}. The first frugal number which is not a [[prime power]] is 1029 = 3 × 7<sup>3</sup>. In [[base 2]], thirty-two is a frugal number, since 32 = 2<sup>5</sup> is written in base 2 as 100000 = 10<sup>101</sup>.

The term '''economical number''' has been used for a frugal number, but also for a number which is either frugal or [[Equidigital number|equidigital]].

==Mathematical definition==
Let <math>b > 1</math> be a number base, and let <math>K_b(n) = \lfloor \log_b{n} \rfloor + 1</math> be the number of digits in a natural number <math>n</math> for base <math>b</math>. A natural number <math>n</math> has the prime factorisation
: <math>n = \prod_{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}} p^{v_p(n)}</math>
where <math>v_p(n)</math> is the [[p-adic valuation|''p''-adic valuation]] of <math>n</math>, and <math>n</math> is an '''frugal number''' in base <math>b</math> if
: <math>K_b(n) > \sum_{{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}}} K_b(p) + \sum_{{\stackrel{p^2 \,\mid\, n}{p\text{ prime}}}} K_b(v_p(n)).</math>
